title: CyberAI Educator Workshop
text:
CORE Center at UA Little Rock · July 29-30, 2026
Two days of practical professional development on AI in the classroom. What the tools can do, where they fail, how to teach with them honestly, and how cybersecurity clinics are putting them to work.

title: CyberAI Educator Workshop
text:
Overview
This workshop brings together classroom educators and cybersecurity clinic practitioners for two days.
Day 1 stays in the classroom. It works through what large language models actually are and aren’t, and the ethics and academic-integrity questions that follow. From there it turns practical: lesson planning, feedback, differentiation, and accessibility. The day closes with what participants still need.
Day 2 turns to cybersecurity clinics: the experiential-learning model behind them, how AI is being integrated into that model, and how three states are running clinics of their own. The afternoon is a hands-on tabletop exercise built on Clinic-in-a-Box.
Materials are posted here as presenters supply them, and they stay up after the workshop.

title: AI Foundations: What Teachers Need to Know
text:
The rest of the workshop assumes you know what these tools actually are, so this is the hour that puts that in place. What a large language model does mechanically, why that explains both what it’s good at and how it fails, and which of the things people commonly believe about them are wrong.
You don’t need a technical background for any of this. The goal is that by the end of the hour you can predict, before you try it, whether a given classroom task is one these tools will handle well.

title: AI Foundations: What Teachers Need to Know
text:
Key points

A language model predicts likely next words. Everything it does well and everything it gets wrong follows from that one fact.
Fluency and accuracy are separate properties. Confident, well-formed, and wrong is the normal failure, not an unusual one.
The reliable rule of thumb: these tools are strong when you supply the content and ask them to change its form, and weak when you ask them to supply the content.
Most of what people believe about how these tools learn, remember, and search is wrong in ways that matter for classroom use.

title: AI Foundations: What Teachers Need to Know
section: What a language model actually does
text:
What a language model actually does
A large language model is a system that has been trained to predict what word comes next, across an enormous amount of text. That’s the whole mechanism. Everything else, the conversation, the essay, the lesson plan, is that prediction running over and over.
Be blunt about what that rules out. The model isn’t looking anything up. It has no database it consults and no notion of a source. When it produces a citation, it’s producing the sequence of words a citation tends to look like. That sequence is sometimes a real paper and sometimes isn’t, and the model has no way to tell the difference, because from the inside there’s no difference.
This is also why the output is so fluent. Fluency is what the training optimizes for. Accuracy comes along for the ride when the training text happened to be accurate and consistent, and it doesn’t when the text was thin, contested, or absent.

title: AI Foundations: What Teachers Need to Know
section: Where it’s strong, where it fails
text:
Where it’s strong, where it fails

Strong: you supply the content, it changes the form
Summarizing a document you paste in. Rewriting your paragraph at a sixth-grade reading level. Turning your rubric into a student-facing checklist. Translating your worksheet. Reformatting your notes into slides. Explaining your own text back to you in different terms.
In all of these the substance is already in front of the model. It isn’t being asked to know anything, only to restate. That’s the task the mechanism is good at, and it’s most of what a teacher needs.


Weak: you ask it to supply the content
Facts it has to recall. Citations. Anything numeric. Recent events. Anything where being almost right is the same as being wrong.
This is the failure that catches people. The model doesn’t know when it doesn’t know. It has no internal signal for the difference between a well-supported answer and a fabricated one, so it delivers both in the same confident register. A human expert hedges when they’re unsure. This won’t.


The rule of thumb
Before you use one of these tools for something, ask where the content is coming from. If it’s coming from you and the tool is changing its shape, you’re on solid ground. If it’s coming from the tool, you have to check it, and checking it often costs more than doing it yourself would have.
That single question predicts most of what you’ll experience in Sessions 4, 5 and 6.

title: AI Foundations: What Teachers Need to Know
text:
Common misconceptions
“It searches the internet.” Usually not. Unless a tool explicitly says it’s browsing or retrieving, it’s generating from training, and the training has a cutoff date.
“It learns from our conversation.” Not in the way people mean. Some products have a memory feature that saves notes about you, but a plain chat doesn’t change the model. Nothing your students type is teaching it.
“It’ll get the math right, it’s a computer.” It’s a language model, not a calculator. Arithmetic is a sequence-prediction problem to it, and it approximates.
“It can tell you whether something was AI-written.” It can’t, and it will confidently say yes or no when asked. More on this in Session 3.
“It understands what it’s saying.” Set this one aside rather than argue it. For classroom purposes the question doesn’t need answering, because the behavior is the same either way, and the behavior is what you’re planning around.

title: AI Disclosure Statements
text:
Most AI policies fail the same way. They’re written once, buried in a syllabus, and phrased so broadly that nobody, including the teacher, can say whether a given use was allowed.
What helps is a specific policy, stated where students will actually run into it, plus the habit of saying what you used yourself. Length has nothing to do with it.
Everything below is meant to be lifted and edited. Nothing here is legal advice or your district’s policy, and where the two conflict, your district wins.

title: AI Disclosure Statements
text:
For your syllabus
Pick the one that matches what you actually want, then say why. The reason is the part students remember.

AI is not permitted
For this course, all submitted work must be your own. Don't use generative AI tools
(ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, and anything like them) to produce text, code, or
images you turn in.

The reason is simple: this course is about building the skill, and you can't build it by
watching something else do it. If you're stuck, come to me. That's what I'm for.

If you're unsure whether a tool counts, ask before you use it, not after.


AI is permitted with disclosure
You may use generative AI tools in this course. If you do, tell me.

Add a short note at the end of anything you submit: which tool, what you asked it for,
and what you did with what it gave you. Two or three sentences is plenty.

Undisclosed AI use is an integrity violation. Disclosed AI use is just how you did the
work, and it won't cost you points.


AI is expected
This course treats AI as a tool you're learning to use well, which means using it, being
honest about it, and being able to defend what came out.

For every assignment, submit your prompts along with your work, and flag anything the tool
produced that you kept without changing. You're responsible for everything you turn in,
including whatever the tool got wrong.

title: AI Disclosure Statements
text:
For a specific assignment
Course-level policies get forgotten by week three. Restating the rule on the assignment itself is what actually works.
AI on this assignment: [allowed / not allowed / allowed for X but not Y]

If allowed, add your disclosure note at the end. If you're not sure whether something
counts, ask me before the due date.
A more specific version, for when the line falls inside the assignment rather than around it:
For this assignment you may use AI to brainstorm, outline, and check your grammar. Don't
use it to write the analysis, which is the part I'm actually grading.

If you used it, say so at the end: which tool, what for.

title: AI Disclosure Statements
text:
For students to use
Give them the words. Most students who don’t disclose aren’t hiding anything, they just don’t know what a disclosure is supposed to look like.
AI use on this assignment: I used [tool] to [what you asked it to do]. I [kept it as is /
rewrote it / used it as a starting point and changed most of it]. Everything else is mine.
Worked examples:
AI use: I used ChatGPT to help me brainstorm topics. I picked one from its list and wrote
the essay myself.
AI use: I used Claude to check my code for errors. It found two bugs and I fixed them. I
wrote the program.
AI use: I used Gemini to draft an outline and then rewrote most of it, because the order it
suggested didn't work for my argument.

title: AI Disclosure Statements
section: For materials you made with AI
text:
For materials you made with AI
This is the one teachers skip, and it’s the one that carries the most weight. If you’re asking students to disclose, disclose.
Parts of this handout were drafted with AI assistance. I reviewed and edited everything
here, and I'm responsible for its accuracy.
A fuller version, for anything going beyond your own classroom:
AI contribution: [tool] was used to [draft / revise / generate examples / format]. All
content was reviewed and edited by [name], who is responsible for its accuracy. AI was not
used to [grade student work / make decisions about students / whatever your line is].

title: AI Disclosure Statements
section: A note on the detection question
text:
A note on the detection question
Don’t build your policy on AI detectors.
They produce false positives, those false positives don’t fall evenly (multilingual writers and students who write in a plain, formulaic style get flagged more often), and a student accused on a detector score has almost no way to prove a negative. A policy that depends on detection puts you in the position of prosecuting a case you can’t actually make.
Policies that hold up are built on process instead: drafts, in-class writing, conversations about the work, and disclosure norms that make honesty the easy path.
This gets covered in more depth in Day 1, Session 3.

title: AI Disclosure Statements
text:
Adapting these
Three things to check before you use any of the above.
Your district or school may already have a policy, and it outranks anything here. Check first.
Say why, not just what. “Don’t use AI” gets ignored. “Don’t use AI, because this assignment exists to build a skill you can’t get any other way” gets followed more often.
Name the tools you mean. “Generative AI” is abstract to a fourteen-year-old. “ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, or anything like them” is not.

title: AI Ethics, Bias & Academic Integrity
text:
Most schools responded to generative AI by buying a detector and writing a policy that points at it. This session argues that both halves of that response are weaker than they look, and that the second one can be fixed. We’ll work through what detection tools actually measure, who gets caught by them and who doesn’t, and how to write a responsible-use policy that survives contact with a real classroom.
Bring a policy if you have one (your school’s, your department’s, or your own syllabus language). You’ll get time to mark it up.

title: AI Ethics, Bias & Academic Integrity
text:
Key points

Detection tools don’t detect AI. They estimate how statistically unsurprising a piece of writing is, which is a different thing.
Tested against a 2015 dissertation and a paragraph written by a language model this month, a commercial detector called both of them human.
Where these tools do err, the errors have historically fallen hardest on the students least able to absorb the cost of being wrongly accused.
A policy that makes detector output the evidence has outsourced an academic-integrity judgment to a vendor.
What holds up is writing permitted use into the assignment, in terms of what the assignment is trying to teach.

title: AI Ethics, Bias & Academic Integrity
text:
The detection problem

Two documents
I ran a test the week before this workshop, and the result is why this session exists in its current form.
The first document was a section of the literature review from my own doctoral dissertation. I wrote it in 2015. There was no large language model available to write it with, so whatever else is true of that text, it can’t contain AI-generated prose.
The second was a paragraph a language model wrote at my direction on the morning of July 27, 2026. I asked it to restate a passage of the same dissertation in plainer language. It’s machine-generated in the most straightforward sense available.
I put both through commercial AI detectors.










Document
Provenance
GPTZero (model 4.7b)
ZeroGPT
Copyleaks




Dissertation literature review, 1,779 words
Human, 2015
100% human
0.6% AI
0% AI


Restated paragraph, 334 words
LLM, July 2026
100% human
0% AI
not yet run



One of those documents couldn’t have been written by a machine. The other couldn’t have been written by anything else. Both tools called both of them human. GPTZero used the same words each time: “We are highly confident this text is entirely human.” Not a hedge, not a maybe. The phrasing a teacher would act on.
Now look at the ordering. ZeroGPT scored the 2015 dissertation at 0.6% AI and the machine-written paragraph at 0%. It didn’t just fail to tell them apart. It ranked them backwards. The one document in the pair that could not possibly contain AI-generated prose is the one it found marginally more suspicious.
The margin is small enough that neither text would be flagged by any sane threshold, and that’s the point. A weak signal you can compensate for by moving the cutoff. An arbitrary ordering leaves you nothing to move.






NoteTwo caveats, since someone will ask





The dissertation was run on GPTZero’s Advanced scan and the paragraph on its Basic scan (the free tier allows one Advanced scan per day). The two documents also differ substantially in length. So two variables moved, not one, and this is a demonstration rather than an experiment.
Note which way the length difference cuts, though. Shorter text gives a detector less to work with, which should make the machine-written paragraph the harder case. It was still called human with high confidence. The confound runs against the tool, not in its favor.





What the tool measures
This isn’t a malfunction. A detector doesn’t recognize machine authorship, because machine authorship leaves no signature to recognize. What it measures is predictability, roughly how closely word choice tracks what a language model would have chosen next. That’s a proxy, and the gap between the proxy and the thing it stands for is where every one of these results lives.
Two things follow that a better version doesn’t fix.
The first is that the signal is weakest where the stakes are highest. A short assignment gives the tool less to work with than a long one, so the scores that matter most in a middle-school classroom are the least reliable ones. OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in 2023 on the grounds that accuracy was too low to be useful. A company with every commercial reason to keep it running concluded it couldn’t.
The second is the base rate, and it’s the part people skip. Suppose a tool is right most of the time, and most students in a class of thirty didn’t use AI. A meaningful share of the flags it raises will still be wrong. The number a vendor quotes is accuracy on their own test set. The number that matters to you is the chance that this flagged student actually did it, and that number is lower, sometimes much lower. That’s the difference between a tool that identifies cheating and a tool that generates a list of students to go and accuse.


Why they now under-flag
There’s a further wrinkle, and it explains the table above. After the false-positive research of 2023 and the press that followed it, vendors recalibrated toward not accusing people. Several now market low false-positive rates as a feature.
That’s the right direction to have moved in. But a detector tuned to almost never accuse falsely is also a detector that almost never catches anything. The trade was sensitivity for safety, and it shifted the worry. Wrongful accusation was the 2023 problem. The 2026 problem is that the tool may be doing nothing for you at all.

title: AI Ethics, Bias & Academic Integrity
text:
Equity
When these tools do get it wrong, the errors aren’t distributed evenly.
Liang and colleagues ran a set of widely used GPT detectors against writing by native and non-native English speakers. The detectors classified the native-speaker samples almost perfectly. They misclassified more than half of the non-native samples as AI-generated.
Two things about that study matter for how much weight to put on it. It’s strong evidence, published, replicated in its own design, mechanistically explained. And it’s from 2023, run against the detectors of that moment. The recalibration described above happened partly because of findings like this one. So treat it as evidence about what these tools do when they’re tuned to catch things, rather than as a current measurement of any particular product.
The mechanism is the part that outlives the vintage. When the researchers enriched the vocabulary in the non-native samples, the misclassification rate fell. When they simplified the native-speaker samples, it rose. The tools are reading lexical range as evidence of humanity, so they penalize a limited English vocabulary and reward a large one, which is a proxy for the thing schools are supposed to be teaching rather than punishing.
Follow that through to the students in front of you. An English learner writes plainly because they’re still acquiring the language. A student using assistive or predictive writing technology under an IEP produces smoothed, conventional prose by design. A student who’s been taught to write to a formula writes to the formula. Each of these is a student doing the thing we asked, and each of them is likelier to be flagged than a confident writer who never had to think about it.
Meanwhile the students who can pay for the better tools are also the students likelier to produce the idiosyncratic prose that reads as human. The tool sorts partly on advantage.
Then consider what an accusation costs. It costs a confident student one uncomfortable conversation. It costs a student who’s already unsure whether they belong considerably more, and some of them don’t come back from it.

title: AI Ethics, Bias & Academic Integrity
text:
Writing a responsible-use policy
The practical half. A policy is doing its job when a student can tell, before starting, what they’re allowed to do, and when you can act on a suspicion without a detector score being your only evidence.
Four things make the difference.

Set the rule per assignment, not per course
Blanket bans fail because they aren’t believed and aren’t enforceable. Blanket permission fails because it doesn’t distinguish between tasks. Whether AI use is acceptable depends on what the specific task is meant to develop, and brainstorming and final prose aren’t the same question.


Say what the assignment is for
“You may not use AI” invites lawyering. “This assignment exists so you practice building an argument from sources, so the argument and the prose need to be yours. Use AI to check your grammar afterwards if you like.” That version tells the student what’s actually being protected, and it holds up when they ask why.


Define disclosure concretely
Name where it goes, what it says, and how long it should be. A one-line note at the end of the document, saying what tool was used and for what, is enough. Unenforced disclosure requirements just teach students that the rules are decorative.


Separate suspicion from evidence
Decide in advance what you do when something looks off, and make the first step a conversation rather than a charge. Ask the student to talk you through their drafting. That conversation is more diagnostic than any score, and it’s survivable when you turn out to be wrong. Which you sometimes will be.






TipTakeaway



Write the rule into the assignment, not into the detector. A policy that explains what the work is for gives students something they can follow and gives you something you can defend. A policy that rests on a similarity score gives you neither.

title: AI Ethics, Bias & Academic Integrity
text:
Resources

title: Lesson Planning, Content Creation, Feedback and Grading
text:
The practical hour. Building lesson materials, differentiating them, and drafting feedback, using AI for the parts of that work where it’s reliable.
This is the session where Session 2’s rule of thumb earns its keep. Nearly everything a teacher wants help with here is a task where you already have the content and you need it in a different shape: a rubric turned into student-facing language, a reading leveled for three different groups, a worksheet built from a text you chose, feedback drafted against work a student handed you. That’s the side of the line where these tools are strong.
Bring something real to work on. A unit you’re teaching this fall, a rubric you’re not happy with, a worksheet you’d like three versions of.

Time

title: Lesson Planning, Content Creation, Feedback and Grading
text:
Key points

The tasks to hand over are the ones where you supply the substance and the tool changes the form. Ask where the content is coming from before you start.
Differentiation is the strongest case in the whole workshop. Producing four versions of one reading at four levels is work teachers rarely have time to do by hand.
Feedback drafting is real help. Grading isn’t the same task, and the difference matters both practically and ethically.
Whatever comes out has your name on it. Check it before it reaches a student.

title: Lesson Planning, Content Creation, Feedback and Grading
text:
Planning and content creation
The reliable pattern is to give the tool your material and ask for a transformation of it. Your unit objectives into a lesson sequence. Your chosen text into comprehension questions. Your rubric into a checklist a fourteen-year-old can actually use. Your slide notes into a handout.
The pattern that disappoints people is asking for the substance itself. “Write me a lesson on the water cycle” produces something generic that you then rewrite, and the rewriting costs about what writing it would have. “Here is my lesson on the water cycle, give me three exit-ticket questions at different difficulty levels” produces something you can use.
Both look like reasonable requests. The second one works because you brought the content.

title: Lesson Planning, Content Creation, Feedback and Grading
text:
Differentiation and accessibility
This is the strongest case in the workshop.
Producing the same reading at three levels, with a vocabulary list for the students who need one, and a version that works with a screen reader, is valuable and time-consuming. Most teachers do a fraction of it, not because they don’t want to but because the day doesn’t contain the hours. This is transformation work of the kind these tools handle well, and the source text is yours.






CautionTwo Cautions



Leveling a text changes it. Check that what came back still says what the original said, particularly with anything technical or historical, because simplification quietly drops qualifiers.
And a simplified text isn’t the same thing as an accommodation. An IEP specifies particular supports, and the fact that a tool can produce something adjacent to one doesn’t mean it satisfies it.

title: Lesson Planning, Content Creation, Feedback and Grading
text:
Feedback and grading
These are different tasks carrying different risks.

Drafting feedback
This one’s a good use. You’ve read the work, you know what you want to say, and you want it written out warmly and at length for thirty students. Give the tool the student’s work and the points you want made, then edit what comes back. The judgment stayed with you.


Assigning a grade
Different thing entirely. A score is a decision about a student, and these tools produce plausible-looking scores with no consistency between runs and no defensible account of how they got there. If a parent asks why their child got a 74, “the model said so” isn’t an answer any of us wants to give.
There’s also a straightforward privacy question. Pasting student work into a commercial tool sends it to a third party, and depending on your district and what’s identifiable in it, that might not be something you’re permitted to do. Check before, not after.
